questions.instruction: Read the complete material and choose the best answer.
questions.prompt: Why might a catalogued interview be unavailable for listening?
questions.hint: Use the complete material and the question together.
questions.material:
Community voices: listening access

The Eastbank Oral History Archive holds recorded interviews about working life in the district. A selection is available in its reading room. Access is intended for research and education; the collection includes personal accounts whose conditions of use vary between recordings.

Register for a free reader account before requesting a visit. State the interview numbers you wish to hear, if known, and explain your research topic. Staff can suggest catalogue entries, but an entry's presence does not guarantee that its audio is currently open for listening. Some recordings remain restricted under the contributor's agreement.

Reading-room sessions last two hours. Headphones and a playback device are provided. You may make written notes, but recording the playback on your own device is not allowed. Where a transcript exists, staff can supply it for consultation alongside the audio. Transcripts may contain corrections or gaps and should not be assumed to preserve every feature of the spoken performance.

Quoting from an interview in a publication requires a separate request. Give the interview reference, proposed extract and intended use. Reader registration alone does not provide that permission. Staff will check the contributor's terms and advise on attribution; they cannot guarantee approval of every extract.

The archive does not charge for listening appointments. Reproduction or research services may involve fees, agreed before work begins. Please cancel an unwanted appointment as early as possible so that the limited listening places can be offered to another reader.

options.text: Catalogue numbers are assigned only after publication
Reader accounts always cost more than the recording
Its contributor’s terms may restrict it
All transcripts automatically replace their audio

questions.instruction: Read the complete material and choose the best answer.
questions.prompt: What does the invented bridge example demonstrate?
questions.hint: Use the complete material and the question together.
questions.material:
The words around the quotation

A short quotation can travel farther than the conversation from which it came. It may appear as a headline, a line in an essay or a sentence shared between friends. Its words can be accurately copied while its meaning is altered by what has been left outside the quotation marks.

Consider an invented exchange about a proposed bridge. Asked whether it should open immediately, an engineer replies, "It is ready, provided the final inspection confirms the work." A headline that quotes only "It is ready" has not changed those four words. It has, however, removed a condition central to what the speaker was willing to claim.

Context is not simply a quantity of extra text. Adding the engineer's favourite breakfast would make the account longer without restoring the missing condition. What matters is information that changes how a reasonable reader understands the claim: the question asked, the qualification given and the issue under discussion.

Nor does every shortened quotation mislead. Writers cannot reproduce every pause or entire interview whenever they refer to a sentence. Selection is unavoidable. The responsibility is to preserve the force of the statement and signal important limits, rather than pretend that completeness is possible or that all omissions are equally serious.

Tone can create another difficulty. An obviously joking remark among friends may look severe in a formal report. Describing it as a joke should also rest on evidence from the exchange, not merely on a later wish to avoid criticism. Context can correct an unfair reading, but it should not become an excuse that automatically protects every speaker.

For readers, the practical response is proportionate curiosity. When a striking quotation carries a large conclusion, ask what surrounding information would matter before accepting it as decisive. The aim is neither suspicion of every quoted word nor unlimited investigation of trivial remarks. It is to recognise that accuracy of transcription and fairness of representation are connected responsibilities, and that one does not automatically fulfil the other.

options.text: Every short quotation contains a spelling error
Inspection is unnecessary whenever an engineer speaks
Longer headlines always solve technical uncertainty
Exact copied words can omit a crucial condition
